segments.title: The Fog and What It Hides: Opening the Case of Bleak House

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, a close reading of one of the most ambitious novels in the English language.
Over this series, we'll be working through Charles Dickens's Bleak House chapter by chapter — its fog, its courts, its secrets, and its extraordinary cast of the doomed and the resilient.
Today we open the case — quite literally at the opening pages — and ask what Dickens is doing from the very first sentence.
Three brilliant guests are joining me throughout this series, and I want to introduce them properly.
First, Dr. Eleanor Hartley — a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism: every gear, every spring, every deliberate choice.
Eleanor, welcome.
Second, Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, Tory of the old school, and a reader who insists that what makes great fiction great is moral imagination, not social programme.
Edmund, delighted to have you.

And finally Dr. Daniel Rosen — cultural historian, who reads every institution in a Dickens novel — the courts, the charities, the great houses — as a mechanism for protecting the powerful at the expense of the poor.
Daniel, wonderful to have you with us.
Let's begin where Dickens begins — with the fog.
What strikes me immediately — every time I return to this opening — is that Dickens doesn't begin with a character or a plot.
He begins with a condition.
The fog isn't backdrop — it's the opening argument of the novel.
Listen to how the passage works — it's almost musical in the way it repeats and descends:

"Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city."
That parenthetical — "and dirty" — is everything.
It's the narrator catching himself, adding the word the polite description left out.
That tiny aside signals we're in the hands of a narrator who will never let gentility obscure the truth.
Eleanor is quite right about the musicality, though I'd describe it rather differently.
The repetition of "fog" is a rhetorical device as old as the Hebrew psalms — anaphora, the tolling of a single word to accumulate weight.
But what moves me is where the fog finally lands.
It descends from grand geography — the Essex marshes, the Kentish heights — and arrives at
"fog cruelly pinching the toes and fingers of his shivering little 'prentice boy on deck."
That is not social criticism — or not primarily.
It is a novelist's instinct to find, in the largest canvas, the single small body that suffers.
I don't want to quarrel with Edmund's reading of the 'prentice boy — it's a genuinely fine observation.
But I think we have to notice what is being mapped here structurally.
The fog doesn't merely descend from high to low — it descends along the lines of social rank.
Greenwich pensioners wheezing by the fireside, the wrathful skipper in his close cabin, and then the boy on deck — each one more exposed than the last.
The fog is indiscriminate in theory and perfectly discriminating in practice.
That is not an accident of Dickens's imagery — that is the argument of the novel announced in its first paragraph.
Daniel puts his finger on something I find thrilling about Dickens's craft here — the way content and form become identical.
The syntax itself performs the social descent he's describing.
And it prepares us for a novel where the mechanisms of power — the law, the great houses, the lawyers — will work in exactly that way.
Think of Tulkinghorn, late in the novel — that extraordinary scene where he lays out his power over Lady Dedlock.
He tells her, with perfect composure:
"I would as soon have hoped to root up by means of my own strength and my own hands the oldest tree on this estate as to shake your hold upon Sir Leicester."
The fog of the opening has, by that chapter, condensed into this man — immovable, patient, pitiless.
Eleanor's connection between the fog and Tulkinghorn is — I confess — rather better than I expected it to be.
What strikes me about that speech is its restraint.
Tulkinghorn isn't raging — he's stating a fact.
"And even now, with this case, I hesitate."
He hesitates — not from mercy, but because he can afford to.
That is the characterisation of a genuinely cold intelligence, and it is Dickens at his most disciplined.
What I want to bring into the room is the other end of that spectrum — not Tulkinghorn's cold restraint, but the novel's surprising moments of warmth.
Because Dickens is always holding both things at once: the system's brutality and the individuals who refuse to be entirely crushed by it.
Mr. Bucket — the detective, a figure of the state's surveillance apparatus — becomes, in one late scene, unexpectedly tender.
He tells Mrs. Rouncewell about her son, and then turns to Sir Leicester and says:

"Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, what you've trusted to me I'll go through with. Don't you be afraid of my turning out of my way, right or left, or taking a sleep, or a wash, or a shave till I have found what I go in search of."
The comedy of that list — sleep, wash, shave — doesn't undercut the vow: it humanises it.
Even the novel's instrument of state power is, at this moment, a man making a promise in the dark.
That image — a man making a promise in the dark — might serve as a description of the novel itself.
Bleak House keeps its promises slowly, and through immense complication — fog, courts, secrets held for decades.
In our next segment, we'll go deeper into the court of Chancery — what it is, what it does, and why Dickens made it the engine of his plot.

segments.title: Richard's Fatal Path: Ambition and Dissolution

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
Today we're turning to one of the novel's most quietly devastating arcs — the slow dissolution of Richard Carstone.
Richard begins the novel as a young man of genuine charm and promise, adored by Ada, trusted by Jarndyce.
But Chancery gets into him like a slow poison, and what we watch is not a villain's rise but a good nature's ruin.
With me today are three extraordinary readers of this novel.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley brings a novelist's eye to the craft — she reads sentences the way a watchmaker reads movements.
Sir Edmund Leigh reads Dickens as a moralist, interested above all in what this story says about individual character and its testing.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen is here to remind us that Richard's failure does not happen in a vacuum — institutions shape destinies, and Chancery is not merely Richard's obsession but his captor.
Let's begin at the beginning of this arc — Chapter Thirteen, where John Jarndyce speaks to Richard and Ada about their love, and sets before them both a warning and a benediction.
What strikes me first about this chapter is how carefully Dickens stages the emotional geometry of it.
Esther describes Richard and Ada placing a chair on either side of her — she becomes literally the hinge between them.
And then she offers this wonderful passage about what the scene felt like — listen to the rhythm of it.
That triplet at the end — constancy, fortitude, perseverance — it's almost liturgical.
Dickens is encoding the very virtues Richard will fail to embody, and doing it through Esther's voice — gently, without melodrama.
It's a kind of dramatic irony so subtle the reader almost doesn't notice it on first reading.
Eleanor is quite right about the irony, and I would press it further.
Those three words — constancy, fortitude, perseverance — are not merely Dickens's programme for a happy marriage.
They are the cardinal virtues of the active moral life, in the classical and the Christian tradition alike.
Richard's tragedy is precisely the failure of will — a failure that is entirely his own, not society's.
Mr. Jarndyce sees it clearly, and says so with a directness that is itself a form of love.
The passage in which he addresses Richard about Providence and effort is among the finest pieces of moral counsel in the novel.
That is not social criticism — that is moral philosophy, and it is addressed to a person, not a class.
I don't disagree that the counsel is beautiful — it is.
But we have to ask: what is the institutional context in which Jarndyce delivers it?
Richard is a ward of Chancery, with no settled profession, no independent income, no stable identity outside the suit.
To tell such a young man to rely on Providence and his own efforts is good advice — but it is advice delivered across a vast structural inequality.
Jarndyce himself is safe — wealthy, established, free from the suit's contamination.
And I think the most unsettling note in this chapter is not in the counsel but in the closing image Esther gives us.
She watches Richard and Ada walk away through sunlit rooms, and the writing does something extraordinary.
The system doesn't announce itself with a villain — it announces itself with a cloud passing over the sun.
That image is doing so much work, and Daniel has put his finger on exactly why.
Esther is not a melodramatic narrator — she resists that.
So when she permits herself this — the room darkening, the sun clouding over — we feel the weight precisely because she has been so restrained.
It's a structural signature Dickens uses across the novel — the physical world briefly aligns with the emotional truth, and then ordinary life resumes.
That gap between the burst of light and the cloud is Richard's entire arc, compressed into three sentences.
And what makes it bearable — just bearable — is Jarndyce's tenderness in the moment before it.
He tells them he imagined their union from afar, and there is something genuinely touching in his confession of that long, quiet hope.
That repetition of 'afar off' is not accidental — it is Jarndyce measuring the distance between hope and its proper season.
He is a man who has learned to want things gently, from a distance, without clutching.
Richard never learns that lesson — and it destroys him.
There is one more passage I want to bring in here, because I think it complicates the purely moral reading.
Jarndyce also tells them — and this is worth attending to — that if they change, if the love fades, they need not be ashamed.
Now — that is a man offering an escape route.
He is telling Richard: you are not bound by a promise made before you knew yourself.
And Richard ignores that too — he stays bound to Ada, but he also stays bound to the suit.
Both attachments become chains — one of flowers, one of lead, exactly as Jarndyce half-predicted.
That image of a chain of flowers becoming a chain of lead — it's one of the novel's quiet prophecies, and none of them hear it.
What's remarkable is that Dickens plants all the evidence of the coming catastrophe here, in Chapter Thirteen, in the warmth and tenderness of this scene.
The sunlight, the hope, the good counsel — and then the room darkens, and they are gone.
In our next segment, we'll be looking at what Chancery actually does to a person — the mechanism of the rot, not just the prognosis.

segments.title: The Secret Beneath: Lady Dedlock's Unravelling

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's great novel apart — slowly, carefully, and with genuine pleasure.
Today we're deep inside one of the novel's most electrically charged threads: the secret life of Lady Dedlock.
With me are three people who know this novel better than almost anyone.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens as a supreme craftsman — alert to every sentence-level decision he makes.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes the novel's greatness lives in its moral imagination — in what it asks of individual character.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian for whom every institution in Bleak House — the law, the aristocracy — is a machine for maintaining power.
Today's question is this: how does Dickens build the suffocating pressure of Lady Dedlock's secret — and what does it reveal about the world she inhabits?
Eleanor, let's start with craft. What is Dickens actually doing, technically, in these passages?
What strikes me first is the absolute precision of the social choreography Dickens stages in these scenes.
He gives us three people in a room — Sir Leicester, Lady Dedlock, Tulkinghorn — and he parcels out attention and knowledge between them with extraordinary control.
Sir Leicester gazes at the fire, blissfully unseeing, while the real drama happens in the air between the other two.
Listen to how Dickens describes their mutual scrutiny — this is from the text of chapter twelve.
'During the utterance of every word of this short dialogue, Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn, without any other alteration in their customary deportment, have looked very steadily at one another.'
That phrase — 'without any other alteration in their customary deportment' — is doing enormous work.
It tells us that the surface is absolutely maintained, even as something seismic passes between them.
Dickens is writing about concealment using the most exposed possible technique — the omniscient narrator who sees everything and tells us precisely what cannot be read.
Eleanor is right about the choreography, and I would add that what makes it devastating is its moral dimension.
Lady Dedlock is a woman of exceptional self-command — and Dickens does not present that as simply admirable.
There is something in her iron composure that is its own kind of deception — of Sir Leicester, of society, of herself.
Dickens gives us this remarkable portrait across their subsequent meetings at Chesney Wold.
'Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine.'
'Exhausted deity' — that is Dickens at the height of his powers. The word 'exhausted' carries genuine spiritual weight here.
She has performed herself so thoroughly and for so long that there is almost nothing left beneath the performance.
That is not a political condition. That is the particular tragedy of a soul that has chosen concealment over truth.
I take Edmund's point about the soul, and I want to honour it — but I think we must ask why she chose concealment, and at whose demand.
Tulkinghorn is not simply a dramatic foil. He is the institutional arm of a ruling class that treats private life as leverage.
Look at how Dickens describes him approaching across the terrace at Chesney Wold.
'He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress.'
He is literally constituted by other people's secrets. They are his substance, his power base, his currency.
And Dickens then gives us this extraordinary line about Tulkinghorn's own interior — whether his soul is devoted to the great, or whether he merely sells them services.
'He is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.'
He is sealed — as perfectly sealed as the class system he serves. That is not incidental. That is the point.
Daniel, that image of Tulkinghorn as sealed — it connects directly to something extraordinary in the syntax of the passage itself.
At the end of chapter twelve, Dickens delivers what I can only call a cascade of unanswered questions.
He sets it up as a series of 'whether' clauses — each one a different dimension of the same unknowable interior.

'Whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows.'
'All this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts.'
That final phrase — 'for the time' — is devastating in its quiet precision. It is a clock ticking.
Dickens structures suspense not through what happens but through what the narrator refuses to resolve.
Eleanor's observation about the 'for the time' is well made — and it connects to something I find philosophically interesting about Sir Leicester's role here.
He is not merely comic. He is genuinely good-natured, in his limited and blinkered fashion.
When he reads out Tulkinghorn's message — fumbling with his eyeglass, losing his place in the letter — the comedy is also pathos.
The message itself is chilling. Listen to how Tulkinghorn phrases it — through Sir Leicester's halting reading.
'I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him.'
'I have seen him.' Three words. The most economical threat in the novel.
And it is delivered, with perfect cruelty, through the unwitting voice of her devoted husband.
Edmund, yes — and what makes that scene so revealing is precisely the institutional structure through which the threat travels.
It goes: Chancery suit, solicitor, affidavit, copied document, the man who copied it.
Every link in that chain is a legal or bureaucratic mechanism — and every one of them is available to Tulkinghorn because of his position.
Lady Dedlock's secret is not simply a personal shame. It is information — and information, in Dickens's world, is power over the body and the life of a woman.
We see the same logic operating in Esther's story — through chapter seventeen, where Jarndyce explains to her how the woman who arranged her upbringing conducted herself.
The arrangement was that the lady — Lady Dedlock, as we understand — would never be seen, never be named.
'That more than this she would never — and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution — for any human consideration disclose.'
The resolution is absolute — and it is driven entirely by terror of exactly the power Tulkinghorn wields.
That passage from Esther's narrative is heartbreaking in a way that I think repays close attention to voice.
Jarndyce says simply: 'My dear, I have told you all.' And that 'all' is devastating precisely because it is so little.
Esther has been given the barest outline of her own origin — filtered through intermediaries, wrapped in legal language, stripped of everything maternal.
Dickens uses the Esther-narrator here with tremendous subtlety — she reports what she was told, and what she was told is a kind of bureaucratic redaction of love.
What I keep returning to, across all these passages, is the symmetry Dickens constructs between Tulkinghorn and Lady Dedlock as sealed containers.
Both are defined by what they will not disclose. And yet they watch each other with absolute intensity.
We've been talking about what the secret reveals about power, about craft, about individual moral life.
In the next segment, we'll look at how this pressure begins to crack — and what the consequences are for everyone caught in its wake.

segments.title: The Lowest Rung: Jo and the Machinery of Indifference

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
I'm joined today by three remarkable minds, each of whom reads Dickens from a very different angle.
Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing scholar who is brilliant on the architecture of Dickens's prose — how the sentences themselves do moral work.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the perspective of a lifetime reading novels as stories about individual character — goodness tested, self-sacrifice, the will under pressure.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen reads Bleak House as an anatomy of power — every institution, every courtroom, every act of charity examined for what it does to the people at the bottom.
Today we're focused on the novel's lowest rung — Jo the crossing-sweeper, the dead man called Nemo, and the women of the brickmakers' yard.
Dickens gives us, in these chapters, something almost unbearable — a tenderness directed at people the world has decided do not count.
Daniel, you've been assigned the passages where Dickens turns his narrator directly on the dead and the discarded — let's begin there.
Thank you.
What Dickens does in chapter eleven is something I find genuinely shocking, even now, having read it many times.
He gives the dead man — this anonymous figure, this Nemo, this nobody — a full past.
A mother who nursed him, perhaps a woman who loved him, a capacity for fire that the world simply extinguished.
And he does it not with sentimentality but with a kind of prosecutorial precision.
Listen to how the passage builds.
"Oh, if in brighter days the now-extinguished fire within him ever burned for one woman who held him in her heart, where is she, while these ashes are above the ground!"
That exclamation point is not grief — it's an indictment.
Dickens is saying: there are people whose entire emotional history — love, connection, the fact of having been a child — is simply erased by poverty and anonymity.
The system doesn't just take their labour or their money.
It takes their legibility as human beings.
The word "ashes" is doing so much work there, isn't it.
You have the literal ashes of a burned-out life — the opium, the degradation — but also ashes in the biblical sense, dust and dissolution.
And then, against those ashes, Dickens places the image of a child's hand, "scarcely knowing how to close upon the neck to which it crept."
That anatomical precision — the hand that doesn't quite know how to grip — is devastating in its specificity.
Dickens understood that the detail that costs the reader most is always the physical one.
Not the argument about poverty, not the statistics — the hand on the neck.
That image persists in the reader's mind long after the chapter is done.
I find myself in rare agreement with Daniel on the force of this passage, though I'd frame it rather differently.
What Dickens insists upon is not a structural critique but a moral demand.
He is asking us — requiring us — to imagine this man as a man, with a history, an inner life, a mother who loved him.
That is a Christian demand, at root — the recognition of the soul in the abandoned figure.
What strikes me equally is the figure of Jo in the later passage — a boy who cannot testify in law, who is literally voiceless before every institution the novel contains.
Yet Dickens says of him, and I want to read this carefully —
"thou art not quite in outer darkness."
That is not a political formulation — that is grace, precisely understood.
I don't want to dismiss grace — but I think the passage earns its tenderness by being precise about what has made Jo so utterly outside the law.
He "can't exactly say" what will happen to him in greater hands — and that phrase is doing double duty.
It captures both Jo's genuine theological ignorance and the inquest's cold dismissal of his testimony.
But then Dickens pivots to the reason Jo keeps vigil over the dead man's grave.
The passage about what Nemo actually gave him is, for me, the moral centre of the whole chapter.
One cold winter night, the man turned, came back, questioned the boy, found he had not a friend in the world, and said —
"Neither have I. Not one!" and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging.
Two people who have nothing — and one of them shares it.
That is the only genuine act of solidarity this novel gives us in these early chapters — and it happens between two people the system has rendered entirely invisible.
What astonishes me about that exchange is the grammar Dickens gives Nemo.
"Neither have I. Not one!" — it's the syntax of a man who was once educated, once precise, now stripped to bare statement.
And then contrast it with Jo's own idiom — "He wos wery good to me, he wos!"
"He wos wery good to me, he wos!"
The spelling itself is a political act — Dickens is recording not just how Jo speaks but what the world has withheld from him.
Jo has never been taught to write, never been taught to read — and yet his moral statement is the clearest in the chapter.
He knows goodness when he experiences it, even if he lacks every word the law would require.
Eleanor puts her finger on something crucial — the hierarchy of eloquence in this chapter is inverted.
Consider, by contrast, Mrs. Piper — who has, as Dickens archly tells us, "a good deal to say, chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation, but not much to tell."
"a good deal to say, chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation, but not much to tell."
The comedy is exquisite — Dickens renders her testimony in a single unpunctuated torrent that mimics the chaos of her speech.
But the comedy has a cutting edge — because Mrs. Piper is the voice of neighbourly opinion, and neighbourly opinion has decided the dead man was dangerous, sinister, not to be mourned.
What Jo knows and Mrs. Piper cannot say is that the man was simply kind.
And kindness, in this novel, is always something that happens outside every official structure — outside the law, outside philanthropy, outside the church.
Which brings me to Jenny and Liz in chapter twenty-two — two women in the brickmakers' yard, bonded by loss.
Jenny has lost a child. Liz fears losing hers.
And in the middle of that grief and that fear, Jenny says something that strikes me as one of the most articulate formulations of solidarity in the entire novel.
She says —

"It's my dead child that makes me love this child so dear, and it's my dead child that makes her love it so dear too... we mean the same thing, if we knew how to say it, us two mothers does in our poor hearts!"
"If we knew how to say it" — there it is again.
The deepest understanding in Bleak House belongs to the people who have been denied the language to express it.
That phrase — "us two mothers does" — is grammatically incorrect and emotionally perfect.
Dickens uses the non-standard verb to signal solidarity — "us" rather than "we," the subject held in the object position, as if even grammar has kept these women subordinate.
And the repetition — "my dead child... my dead child... love it so dear... love it so dear" — that's not careless; it's incantatory.
Jenny is constructing, out of her own grief, a theory of empathy — and she's doing it walking up and down, nursing another woman's baby.
What Dickens gives these women is precisely what he refuses to give the institutions of the novel — the capacity for genuine feeling.
Chancery deliberates endlessly and feels nothing. Mrs. Jellyby organises at vast scale and feels nothing.
But Jenny, walking up and down in a brickmaker's yard, carrying a child not her own, has reasoned her way — through grief — to a complete moral philosophy.
I find that one of the most quietly devastating things in the whole of Bleak House.
That word "quietly" feels exactly right for this whole cluster of passages — a devastation that doesn't announce itself.
Jo who can't testify, Nemo who has no name, Jenny who doesn't know the words — and yet between them they carry more moral weight than the entirety of the Court of Chancery.
In our next segment, we turn to the question of how Bleak House constructs its institutions — Chancery, philanthropy, the law — and what Dickens imagines could, or could not, replace them.

segments.title: Systems of Entrapment: Class, Law, and Complicity

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the series in which we move through Dickens's great novel chapter by chapter, with three extraordinary readers alongside me.
I'm your host, and today's segment takes us into some of the novel's darkest territory — systems of entrapment: class, law, and complicity.
With us today are three voices who bring very different lenses to bear on this material.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a movement — with delight in every gear.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose conviction that the novel is above all a moral drama — about character, conscience, and self-sacrifice — keeps us honest about what stories are actually for.

And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every institution in Dickens — the law, the great house, the family — as a mechanism of class power, and argues that Dickens was more radical than even he knew.
Daniel, I want to start with you — because the passages before us today cut right to the heart of your argument about how systems sustain themselves.
Thank you — and yes, these passages together form something like an anatomy of the novel's entire argument about power.
Dickens gives us the most nakedly polemical statement in the whole of Bleak House in Chapter Thirty-Nine, and it's worth reading it exactly as he wrote it.
"The one great principle of the English law is to make business for itself."
There is no hedging there, no irony — that is the narrator stepping forward and stating the verdict plainly.
And then comes the extraordinary twist: Dickens says that if the public once understood this principle clearly, they would, quote, "cease to grumble."
That is savage satire — the system's victims would acquiesce if only they grasped the logic of their own exploitation.
It's not merely a complaint about lawyers' fees — it is an argument that the law is constitutively predatory, that self-perpetuation is its DNA.
What strikes me as a craftsperson is the rhetorical move Dickens makes there — the false consolation of comprehension.
He writes that the law becomes, viewed by its own light, quote, "a coherent scheme and not the monstrous maze the laity are apt to think it."
The word "coherent" is doing corrosive work — because coherence, normally a virtue, here becomes the mark of something perfectly, chillingly organised against you.
Dickens understood that the most oppressive systems are not chaotic — they are legible, self-consistent, and therefore unassailable from within.
I will grant the force of that reading — Dickens's indictment of Chancery is the most sustained piece of institutional satire in the English novel.
But I would press back, gently, on the idea that the system is the novel's deepest subject.
Look at the passage George Rouncewell moves through in Chapter Fifty-Eight — alone in the great house, carrying his lamp.
Dickens writes of George's thoughts — the murdered man, the vanished lady, the stricken master upstairs — and then tells us George reflects
"how he MIGHT see something now, which it would tax his boldness to walk up to, lay his hand upon, and prove to be a fancy."
That is not a passage about class — it is a passage about conscience, about what a man fears to find when he looks directly at what he half suspects.
The terror George feels is personal, moral, human — not structural.
Edmund, I think those two readings aren't as opposed as they look — and the passage itself shows why.
George is haunted by the murdered man whose image is, the narrator tells us, fresh in his mind — and by the lady who has disappeared.
But what finally greets him?
Dickens writes: "it is all blank, blank as the darkness above and below."
That blankness is the system's answer to individual guilt — it absorbs it, it buries it, it leaves nothing to lay your hand upon.
Conscience, without structural change, walks upstairs and finds nothing it can grasp.
There's a figure in the novel who embodies that blankness even more completely than an empty house — and that is Tulkinghorn.
The passage in Chapter Eleven is, for me, one of the most technically perfect in Bleak House.
Dickens describes him standing by the portmanteau — "equally removed, to all appearance" from professional interest, pious feeling, and human awe.
And then comes the sentence that clinches it — listen to the comparison Dickens reaches for:
"As easily might the tone of a delicate musical instrument be inferred from its case, as the tone of Mr. Tulkinghorn from his case."
The word "case" does double duty — a legal case, a carrying case, a shell — and Dickens has just told us that Tulkinghorn has shown nothing but his shell.
This is craft at the level of a great poem — every word load-bearing.
And yet — and Eleanor, I think you'll allow me this — what Dickens is describing in Tulkinghorn is not merely a social function.
He is a study in what happens to the inner life when a man devotes himself entirely to other people's secrets — when he becomes, as it were, only a vessel.
The narrator notes he has shown "neither patience nor impatience, nor attention nor abstraction" — and that list of negatives is a moral portrait, not merely a social one.
Johnson observed that the law sharpens the mind by narrowing it — Tulkinghorn is the awful proof of that narrowing carried to its terminus.
That narrowing, though, serves a function — and the function is the protection of aristocratic secrets, the maintenance of Dedlock power.
Which brings me to the passage I find the most devastating in this group — Mrs. Rouncewell's account of the historical Lady Dedlock in Chapter Seven.
Here is a woman who has married into the wrong side — her brother killed by the very family she's been absorbed into.
Her resistance — sabotaging the horses of the king's cause — is the only form of political agency available to her, and it is furtive, nocturnal, bodily.
And the consequence is told with the economy of a sentence:
"she was lamed in the hip and from that hour began to pine away."
The body is the site where class and gender power exact their final cost — she is literally crippled by the structure she tried to resist.
And Dickens threads that same logic of bodily sacrifice through the passage John Jarndyce narrates about Lady Dedlock's sister in Chapter Forty-Three.
This is Esther's narration of Jarndyce's account — already twice mediated — and the language is almost unbearably compressed.
Jarndyce tells us she wrote to Boythorn, and the letter is described not summarised — here is what she wrote:

"she wrote him that from the date of that letter she died to him — as in literal truth she did — and that the resolution was exacted from her by her knowledge of his proud temper and his strained sense of honour, which were both her nature too."
"Died to him" — the metaphor has become literal, and she knows it even as she writes.
That phrase "strained sense of honour, which were both her nature too" — she shares the very quality that destroys her.
That is the passage in this entire group that moves me most deeply — and I think Daniel will forgive me for saying that no class analysis fully accounts for it.
She made the sacrifice, Jarndyce says, and Dickens gives us the full weight of those words:
"she made the sacrifice, she said, and would live in it and die in it."
"She did both." — Jarndyce adds, and those two words close the door on the whole of a life.
That is a story about pride, honour, and self-immolation — which are ancient human things, and no law made them.
Edmund, I won't quarrel with the emotion — it is devastating.
But I'd note that the pride Jarndyce describes — "his proud temper and his strained sense of honour" — is not universal human nature.
It is the specific moral code of a class — one that treats a woman's reputation as a property right to be protected by her own destruction.
What the system cannot accommodate, it requires its victims to eliminate — themselves.
That tension — between individual moral tragedy and the systems that shape and sometimes require it — may be the very thing that keeps Bleak House alive after nearly two centuries.
We've moved from the frozen solicitor by his portmanteau to a woman who wrote her own death sentence — and in every case, the law, the house, the code of honour all hold the walls up.
In our next segment we'll turn to the question of how Dickens structures our sympathy — who gets to suffer visibly in this novel, and why.

segments.title: Dickens's Art: How Form Mirrors Chaos

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme where we take Dickens's vast, magnificent novel apart — very carefully — to see how it works.
I'm your host, and today we're asking a question that sits at the heart of the whole enterprise: how does Dickens make form mirror chaos?
The novel is famously unruly — two narrators, dozens of characters, plotlines that sprawl across decades — and yet every page feels controlled, purposeful, shaped.
To help us think through that, I'm joined by three extraordinary readers of this novel.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose great gift is making the craft of fiction feel thrilling — she sees the architecture behind the prose.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads Dickens as a moralist first — a chronicler of character tested by circumstance — and whose beautifully measured judgements we'll be relying on throughout.

And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every institution in the novel — the law, the aristocracy, philanthropy — as a mechanism of class power, and who brings fierce, evidence-driven energy to the table.
Let's begin with a passage that feels almost like Dickens showing his hand — the Tom-all-Alone's scene, where the omniscient narrator takes us into the worst slum in London.
Eleanor, that passage is yours — what do you see there?
What strikes me first — and it never stops striking me — is the parenthesis.
Dickens drops this aside into the middle of the street description, almost casually, and it's where all the moral weight lands.
The sentence reads — and I want to read it whole because the shape of it matters:

"a villainous street, undrained, unventilated, deep in black mud and corrupt water — though the roads are dry elsewhere — and reeking with such smells and sights that he, who has lived in London all his life, can scarce believe his senses."
"Though the roads are dry elsewhere" — four words embedded in a dash, and they detonate the whole thing.
This is not the weather, not some Gothic atmospheric accident — this is a chosen condition, sustained against the normal order of things.
And then Dickens locks the reader inside the viewpoint of a man who has lived in London all his life and still cannot believe what he sees.
That is the formal stroke of genius: familiarity made strange, and strangeness made inexcusable.
Eleanor's right about the parenthesis, and I want to push on what that parenthesis is actually saying politically.
The roads are dry elsewhere — meaning, the rest of the city's infrastructure functions.
The drainage, the ventilation, the clean water — those things exist, they are available, but they have been withheld from this particular street and these particular people.
And Dickens underlines that with the progression into the deeper streets — branching from this street are other courts so infamous that Snagsby feels he is descending into an infernal gulf.
The Gothic imagery isn't decorative — it is the novel's argument about what organised neglect produces.
Hell is not a metaphor here — it is a policy outcome.
I won't quarrel with the observation, though I'd resist the conclusion.
What Dickens achieves in that passage is something rather more ancient than a political argument — it is the literary sublime pressed into service of conscience.
Snagsby descends not into a policy failure but into a vision of what human beings are capable of doing to one another — which is a moral and spiritual horror before it is an administrative one.
The form serves that — the accumulating clauses, the Gothic descent — because nothing else could convey the sheer weight of it.
Now, I find the counterpoint in the Boythorn passage rather interesting in that respect.
If Tom-all-Alone's shows us form straining under tragic weight, Boythorn shows us the same formal energy — that same relentless accumulation — deployed in pure comedy.
Listen to how Dickens builds the legal sparring to its climax:
"He brings actions for trespass; I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha, ha!"
The parallel syntax, the perfect legal mirroring, and then that laughter — it is a tiny, perfectly-engineered joke about the whole machinery of English law.
Edmund has put his finger on something I think is absolutely central to how Bleak House works as a formal object.
Dickens keeps deploying the same structural gesture — that piling-up, that relentless catalogue — and each time the emotional register shifts entirely.
In Boythorn's account, the accumulation is exhilarating — fire engines, humane man-traps, chopped gates burned by morning — the man's fury is magnificent and absurd at once.
But the same technique in Tom-all-Alone's — heaps of ruins, branching streets, courts so infamous — becomes unendurable.
It's one writer's signature, doing two entirely different things with the same hand.
And it's not a coincidence that both passages involve a confrontation with an institution that is supposed to dispense justice and instead amplifies power.
Boythorn's comedy works because he can afford to treat the law as a game — he has the resources to fire back, literally and legally.
The people of Tom-all-Alone's have no fire engine — they have only the corrupt water and the unventilated dark.
Dickens is placing these two scenes in the same novel deliberately — the farce illuminates the tragedy by contrast.
That structural juxtaposition is, I'd argue, the most radical thing about the architecture of Bleak House.
I shall not dispute the juxtaposition — though I suspect Dickens would have been surprised to hear himself called a structural radical.
He was doing what a great storyteller does: using every register available to him to keep the reader in a state of alert attention.
I want to add one further dimension — the Tulkinghorn passage — because there the formal compression becomes almost unbearable.
Dickens gives Tulkinghorn almost nothing to do physically — he does not stir hand or foot, does not raise his voice.
And yet the threat he delivers is total:
"Lady Dedlock, have the goodness to stop and hear me, or before you reach the staircase I shall ring the alarm-bell and rouse the house."
The form enacts the power: absolute stillness producing absolute control — that is Dickens at his most frightening.
That Tulkinghorn passage is one I return to again and again, because of exactly that stillness.
Lady Dedlock moves — she reaches for the inner door, she takes it in her hand — and every one of those small physical gestures is the novel giving her the appearance of agency.
And then the narrator tells us: Tulkinghorn does this without himself stirring hand or foot or raising his voice.
That syntactic negative — without — does the work that a whole scene of physical struggle would do in a lesser novel.
One word and the power relation is established, permanently, in the reader's nervous system.
And notice what the threat actually is: to expose her secret before every guest and servant, every man and woman in the house.
The alarm-bell is the instrument of a social order that runs on reputation, on rank, on the performance of respectability.
Tulkinghorn doesn't need physical force — the machinery of class surveillance does the work for him.
That is why the Richard Carstone thread matters so much alongside all of this.
Mrs. Badger's assessment of Richard is devastating precisely because it is delivered in the mildest, most reasonable tones:

"Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
Woodcourt earns his vocation; Richard floats on the system's promises and sinks when those promises prove empty — the novel has designed that contrast with precision.
That contrast is, I think, Dickens at his most serious as a moralist.
Woodcourt's vocation — genuine, unsentimentalised, bought at considerable personal cost — is the positive against which Richard's vacancy is measured.

Richard doesn't fail because the system corrupts him, though the system certainly doesn't help — he fails because he cannot find, within himself, the kind of positive interest that makes work worthwhile.
That is a very old moral truth, and Dickens renders it with complete clarity and no sentimentality whatsoever.
What I find formally remarkable about Mrs. Badger's speech is its indirectness — she never says Richard will fail outright.
She says he lacks positive interest, that he finds it tiresome — and then draws the contrast with Woodcourt so precisely that the reader draws the conclusion before she states it.
That's characterisation by implication — the form of the speech performing the very quality it describes: good judgment delivered without flourish.
What's extraordinary about this conversation is how consistently we've found Dickens doing the same thing: using form to do the work that lesser novelists leave to explicit statement.

The parenthesis in Tom-all-Alone's, the stillness of Tulkinghorn, the parallel syntax of Boythorn's laughter, the gentle precision of Mrs. Badger's verdict on Richard — all of it structural, all of it moral.

In our next segment, we'll be looking at how that moral architecture plays out across the two narrators — the omniscient voice and Esther's first person — and what Dickens risks by dividing the novel's consciousness in two.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Redemption and Ruin: What Bleak House Leaves Us With

utterances.text: We've arrived at the final stretch of our conversation about Bleak House, and I think it's the right moment to ask what the novel ultimately leaves us with.
Not resolution, exactly — Dickens isn't that kind of novelist.
But there are characters whose fates feel like verdicts — on the law, on class, on the possibility of goodness surviving in a corrupted world.
Edmund, I'd like to begin with you — because you've been our guide to moral imagination throughout, and the closing chapters seem to demand exactly that.
Thank you. What strikes me most, returning to the novel's close, is how mercilessly Dickens exposes the gap between how power sees itself and how it actually operates.
Consider Lady Dedlock — a figure of immense self-possession, or so she believes.
Dickens tells us, with devastating precision, that she supposes herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of ordinary mortals.
And yet every tradesperson, every deferential lackey around her, has her entirely mapped.
Dickens puts it with a Swiftian flourish — and I mean that as the highest compliment — when he writes of those who lead her and her whole troop after them.
"who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput."
That is not satire in the modern, knowing sense — it is moral comedy of the deepest kind.
The grandeur is real, and its hollowness is equally real, and the genius is in holding both together without condescension.
I think Edmund is right that there's genuine moral comedy there — but I'd press on what the comedy is actually revealing.
Blaze and Sparkle, Sheen and Gloss, Mr. Sladdery — these aren't just satirical grotesques.
They are the market — they are the mechanism by which aristocratic taste is manufactured and sold back to itself.
Lady Dedlock believes she leads fashion; in fact she is its most profitable product.
And the novel's structural genius — this is where I think Eleanor would agree — is that this satire of the top is mirrored by genuine tragedy at the bottom.
Gridley — the man from Shropshire — is the clearest image of what the system actually produces when it has finished with a person.
He tells us himself, and the language is unforgettable:
"I have been dragged for five and twenty years over burning iron, and I have lost the habit of treading upon velvet."
Twenty-five years. Chancery did not merely ruin him financially — it reconfigured his entire capacity for ordinary human softness.
That phrase — burning iron — is the kind of thing that stops you mid-page, because it's so bodily, so physical, in a novel full of legal abstraction.
Chancery is all paperwork and delay and impersonal cruelty — and Gridley translates it back into flesh and nerve.
That's a profound craft choice by Dickens: the system is abstract, but its victims are irreducibly concrete.
And it connects, I think, to the tragedy of Richard Carstone — which is the one that undoes me every time.
Because Richard isn't destroyed by malice or poverty — he's destroyed by inconstancy, by an inability to hold his own shape against the gravitational pull of the suit.
He confesses it to Esther with an almost unbearable self-awareness:
"My dear Esther, I understand you, and I wish to heaven I were a more constant sort of fellow."

"If I were a more constant sort of fellow, I should have held on either to Badger or to Kenge and Carboy like grim death, and should have begun to be steady and systematic by this time, and shouldn't be in debt."
He knows exactly what he is — and that knowledge does nothing to save him.
Eleanor has put her finger on something that I think is the novel's most searching moral question.
Self-knowledge without will — is that tragedy, or is it a kind of moral failure?
Richard is not wicked. He is weak — and Dickens is too honest a novelist to pretend that weakness is innocence.
The great tradition of the novel — from Fielding through to Austen — has always understood that character is destiny.
Chancery is the occasion for Richard's ruin, but inconstancy is its cause.
I won't entirely resist that — character matters — but I'd want to ask what shapes character in the first place.
Richard grows up under the shadow of Jarndyce and Jarndyce. It is the structuring fact of his existence from childhood.
The suit doesn't merely distract him — it provides the only horizon he can imagine.
When he says he wishes to be constant to himself — not to Ada, to himself — that word, himself, is doing enormous work.
Because Chancery has colonised his self. There is no self left that is fully free of it.
And that, I think, is why Esther's narration is so crucial to the architecture of the novel.
She records Richard's confession with absolute fidelity — no judgment, no editorialising — but the very plainness of her account is devastating.
Dickens understood that restraint in a narrator can be a form of amplification.
The more quietly Esther watches, the louder the tragedy becomes.
What I hear across all three of your readings is a novel that refuses comfort — that is rigorous about the costs of being human in a broken world.
Lady Dedlock's grandeur hollowed out from within, Gridley ground down by twenty-five years of legal iron, Richard dissolving into a suit that was never his salvation.
And yet — as you've all shown — the novel's unflinching clarity is itself a kind of moral act.
To see clearly, Dickens seems to say, is the beginning of whatever redemption is available to us.
My thanks to Dr. Eleanor Hartley, Sir Edmund Leigh, and Dr. Daniel Rosen for a conversation of genuine depth and feeling.
And thank you for listening to Bleak House Unpacked.

Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and
meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers
of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city.
Fog on the Essex marshes, fog on the Kentish heights. Fog creeping
into the cabooses of collier-brigs; fog lying out on the yards and
hovering in the rigging of great ships; fog drooping on the gunwales
of barges and small boats. Fog in the eyes and throats of ancient
Greenwich pensioners, wheezing by the firesides of their wards; fog
in the stem and bowl of the afternoon pipe of the wrathful skipper,
down in his close cabin; fog cruelly pinching the toes and fingers of
his shivering little ’prentice boy on deck. Chance people on the
bridges peeping over the parapets into a nether sky of fog, with fog
all round them, as if they were up in a balloon and hanging in the
misty clouds.

there must be a lapse of several years before this early love could
come to anything, and how it could come to happiness only if it were
real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do
their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and
perseverance, each always for the other’s sake. Well! Richard said

she would work her fingers to the bone for Richard, and they called
me all sorts of endearing and sensible names, and we sat there,

“Come!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “Now for our assumption. Now we lift our
eyes up and look hopefully at the distance! Rick, the world is before
you; and it is most probable that as you enter it, so it will receive
you. Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never
separate the two, like the heathen waggoner. Constancy in love is a
good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy
in every kind of effort. If you had the abilities of all the great
men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely
meaning it and setting about it. If you entertain the supposition
that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could
be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts,
leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here.”

“Well!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “That’s rational. Now, hear me, my dears!
I might tell you that you don’t know your own minds yet, that a
thousand things may happen to divert you from one another, that it is
well this chain of flowers you have taken up is very easily broken,
or it might become a chain of lead. But I will not do that. Such
wisdom will come soon enough, I dare say, if it is to come at all. I
will assume that a few years hence you will be in your hearts to one
another what you are to-day. All I say before speaking to you
according to that assumption is, if you DO change—if you DO come to
find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and
woman than you were as boy and girl (your manhood will excuse me,
Rick!)—don’t be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be
nothing monstrous or uncommon in it. I am only your friend and
distant kinsman. I have no power over you whatever. But I wish and
hope to retain your confidence if I do nothing to forfeit it.”

c39:p3.text:
The one great principle of the English law is to make business for
itself. There is no other principle distinctly, certainly, and
consistently maintained through all its narrow turnings. Viewed by
this light it becomes a coherent scheme and not the monstrous maze
the laity are apt to think it. Let them but once clearly perceive
that its grand principle is to make business for itself at their
expense, and surely they will cease to grumble.
c39:p3.summary: The narrator explicitly argues that English law's fundamental principle is self-perpetuation and profit-generation, and that if the public understood this, they would cease complaining about its absurdities.

c58:p98.text:
The trooper, his old recollections awakened by the solitary grandeur
of a great house—no novelty to him once at Chesney Wold—goes up the
stairs and through the chief rooms, holding up his light at arm’s
length. Thinking of his varied fortunes within the last few weeks,
and of his rustic boyhood, and of the two periods of his life so
strangely brought together across the wide intermediate space;
thinking of the murdered man whose image is fresh in his mind;
thinking of the lady who has disappeared from these very rooms and
the tokens of whose recent presence are all here; thinking of the
master of the house upstairs and of the foreboding, “Who will tell
him!” he looks here and looks there, and reflects how he MIGHT see
something now, which it would tax his boldness to walk up to, lay his
hand upon, and prove to be a fancy. But it is all blank, blank as the
darkness above and below, while he goes up the great staircase again,
blank as the oppressive silence.
c58:p98.summary: George patrols the grand house, his memories of past and present mingling, sensing the shadows of the missing Lady Dedlock and the murdered Tulkinghorn, finding only emptiness.

appearance, from all three kinds of interest exhibited near the
bed—from the young surgeon’s professional interest in death,
noticeable as being quite apart from his remarks on the deceased as

are dry elsewhere—and reeking with such smells and sights that he,
who has lived in London all his life, can scarce believe his senses.

c9:p49.text:
“By my soul,” exclaimed Mr. Boythorn, suddenly firing another volley,
“that fellow is, and his father was, and his grandfather was, the
most stiff-necked, arrogant imbecile, pig-headed numskull, ever, by
some inexplicable mistake of Nature, born in any station of life but
a walking-stick’s! The whole of that family are the most solemnly
conceited and consummate blockheads! But it’s no matter; he should
not shut up my path if he were fifty baronets melted into one and
living in a hundred Chesney Wolds, one within another, like the ivory
balls in a Chinese carving. The fellow, by his agent, or secretary,
or somebody, writes to me ‘Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, presents
his compliments to Mr. Lawrence Boythorn, and has to call his
attention to the fact that the green pathway by the old
parsonage-house, now the property of Mr. Lawrence Boythorn, is Sir
Leicester’s right of way, being in fact a portion of the park of
Chesney Wold, and that Sir Leicester finds it convenient to close up
the same.’ I write to the fellow, ‘Mr. Lawrence Boythorn presents his
compliments to Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, and has to call HIS
attention to the fact that he totally denies the whole of Sir
Leicester Dedlock’s positions on every possible subject and has to
add, in reference to closing up the pathway, that he will be glad to
see the man who may undertake to do it.’ The fellow sends a most
abandoned villain with one eye to construct a gateway. I play upon
that execrable scoundrel with a fire-engine until the breath is
nearly driven out of his body. The fellow erects a gate in the night.
I chop it down and burn it in the morning. He sends his myrmidons to
come over the fence and pass and repass. I catch them in humane man
traps, fire split peas at their legs, play upon them with the
engine—resolve to free mankind from the insupportable burden of the
existence of those lurking ruffians. He brings actions for trespass;
I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and
battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha,
ha!”
c9:p49.summary: Boythorn launches an elaborate account of his escalating disputes with Sir Leicester over a right of way, detailing the volleys of letters, his theatrical retaliation with a fire engine, his destruction of gates, and the counter-actions in law, all recounted with relish and concluding with triumphant laughter.

c2:p12.text:
Has Mr. Tulkinghorn any idea of this himself? It may be so, or it may
not, but there is this remarkable circumstance to be noted in
everything associated with my Lady Dedlock as one of a class—as one
of the leaders and representatives of her little world. She supposes
herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of
ordinary mortals—seeing herself in her glass, where indeed she looks
so. Yet every dim little star revolving about her, from her maid to
the manager of the Italian Opera, knows her weaknesses, prejudices,
follies, haughtinesses, and caprices and lives upon as accurate a
calculation and as nice a measure of her moral nature as her
dressmaker takes of her physical proportions. Is a new dress, a new
custom, a new singer, a new dancer, a new form of jewellery, a new
dwarf or giant, a new chapel, a new anything, to be set up? There are
deferential people in a dozen callings whom my Lady Dedlock suspects
of nothing but prostration before her, who can tell you how to manage
her as if she were a baby, who do nothing but nurse her all their
lives, who, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience,
lead her and her whole troop after them; who, in hooking one, hook
all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet
of the majestic Lilliput. “If you want to address our people, sir,”
say Blaze and Sparkle, the jewellers—meaning by our people Lady
Dedlock and the rest—“you must remember that you are not dealing
with the general public; you must hit our people in their weakest
place, and their weakest place is such a place.” “To make this
article go down, gentlemen,” say Sheen and Gloss, the mercers, to
their friends the manufacturers, “you must come to us, because we
know where to have the fashionable people, and we can make it
fashionable.” “If you want to get this print upon the tables of my
high connexion, sir,” says Mr. Sladdery, the librarian, “or if you
want to get this dwarf or giant into the houses of my high connexion,
sir, or if you want to secure to this entertainment the patronage of
my high connexion, sir, you must leave it, if you please, to me, for
I have been accustomed to study the leaders of my high connexion,
sir, and I may tell you without vanity that I can turn them round my
finger”—in which Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not
exaggerate at all.
c2:p12.summary: Despite believing herself inscrutable, Lady Dedlock is perfectly understood and managed by tradespeople and servants who deliberately lead her and her circle by flattery and careful study of her preferences.
c2:p12.best_quote: who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput
